paragraphs: This paper investigates whether much deeper neural networks can improve self-supervised reinforcement learning. The agent receives neither demonstrations nor rewards: it must explore from scratch and learn to reach goals when commanded. The central question is whether increasing network depth changes what an agent can learn in this demanding setting.

The researchers study building blocks that make this learning process scale, identifying depth as a critical factor. Whereas recent reinforcement learning systems commonly use roughly two to five layers, their experiments increase depth to as many as 1,024 layers. They evaluate the approach on simulated locomotion and manipulation tasks using self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning.

The reported performance improvements range from twofold to fiftyfold over the contrastive reinforcement learning algorithm, with results exceeding other goal-conditioned baselines. Deeper networks also produce qualitative changes in learned behavior, beyond higher success rates alone. These findings establish depth as a promising source of additional goal-reaching capabilities in the tested self-supervised setting.
neurips-2025-1000-layer-networks-for-sel.tldr: Networks up to 1,024 layers deep substantially improve self-supervised goal-reaching performance and change learned behaviors in simulated tasks.

paragraphs: Time normalization turns expressions about time into representations that software can use. The difficult cases include expressions composed from several parts, times defined relative to events, and expressions spread across multiple text spans. The paper argues that traditional systems based on ISO-TimeML have limited ability to represent these constructions.

The proposed approach treats normalization as generating executable code. It uses SCATE, a framework whose symbolic operators express how temporal meanings combine, and implements those operators in a Python library. Large language models generate SCATE programs, allowing temporal interpretations to take an explicit, executable form rather than remaining only textual answers.

The authors also use large language models to generate annotated training data, with validation at the code level. Small models trained on this augmented data achieve strong experimental performance and outperform the larger models that generated their training examples. This combination connects expressive temporal representations with locally deployable models, making the resulting interpretations practical to compute and easier to inspect.
neurips-2025-a-semantic-parsing-framewor.tldr: Executable temporal code and validated synthetic training data let small local models outperform their LLM teachers at time normalization.

paragraphs: AgroMind evaluates how well large multimodal models understand agricultural remote sensing images. The authors identify two weaknesses in existing agricultural benchmarks: limited scene diversity and tasks that are too simple. Their benchmark broadens evaluation across spatial perception, object understanding, scene understanding, and reasoning about scenes.

The evaluation set combines nine public datasets with one private global parcel dataset, producing 28,482 question-answer pairs across 20,850 images. Its thirteen task types cover topics including crop identification, health monitoring, and environmental analysis. Building the benchmark involves standardizing source data, refining annotations, and systematically designing questions tied to agricultural tasks.

The authors evaluate twenty open-source models and four closed-source models. Results reveal substantial performance gaps, particularly in spatial reasoning and fine-grained recognition, while several leading models outperform the evaluated human performance. These findings show that strong overall capability can coexist with specific agricultural weaknesses. AgroMind provides a standardized way to examine those differences and identify where domain understanding remains inadequate.
neurips-2025-can-large-multimodal-models.tldr: AgroMind benchmarks agricultural image understanding and exposes weaknesses in spatial reasoning and fine-grained recognition across multimodal models.

paragraphs: When one class has relatively few examples, synthetic oversampling creates additional minority-class training samples. SMOTE and related methods are widely used for this purpose, but their practical success has outpaced theoretical understanding. This paper develops a framework for analyzing classifiers trained with these artificially generated examples.

Its first result bounds the discrepancy between error measured on synthetic minority samples and error on the actual minority population. The bound is uniform, providing control beyond the error of a single fixed classifier. This addresses a central issue in oversampling: good performance on generated examples needs a theoretical connection to performance on the distribution those examples are intended to represent.

The authors then establish an excess-risk guarantee for nonparametric kernel-based classifiers trained with synthetic data. Together, the results yield guidance for choosing parameters of both the oversampling procedure and the downstream classifier. Numerical experiments illustrate and support the theory, connecting the mathematical analysis to practical decisions about how synthetic minority examples should be used.
neurips-2025-concentration-and-excess-ri.tldr: The paper derives theoretical guarantees linking SMOTE-generated training data to minority-population error and kernel-classifier performance.

paragraphs: Deep Edge Filter introduces a deliberately designed filtering operation for the internal features of neural networks. Its motivation is a hypothesis about where different information resides: task-relevant meaning may occupy high-frequency feature components, while biases specific to a domain may occupy low-frequency components. The method aims to improve generalization by separating these contributions.

The operation first obtains a low-pass filtered version of a feature representation and subtracts it from the original. This leaves the high-frequency component while preserving the surrounding network architecture. The intervention therefore targets the representation itself, applying the same basic filtering idea across different kinds of models and input data.

Experiments in vision, text, three-dimensional data, and audio report consistent improvements across the architectures and modalities studied. Additional analysis finds that the filter makes features sparser and isolates high-frequency components, providing empirical support for the motivating hypothesis. The results suggest that a human-designed feature transformation can usefully complement learned representations across diverse tasks.
neurips-2025-deep-edge-filter-return-of-.tldr: A high-pass filter on internal neural features improves generalization across tested modalities, supporting a frequency-based hypothesis about useful features and domain biases.

paragraphs: DMol generates small drug molecules using diffusion over molecular graphs. The approach addresses both the number of generation steps and the preservation of important chemical patterns. Its central design choice is to represent selected carbon rings and other relevant motifs as supernodes, keeping these structures together during generation and allowing their subsequent integration into a molecular scaffold.

The model also combines deterministic and random perturbations of subgraphs, coupling the noise schedules for nodes and edges. Its training loss is modified to exploit the deterministic part of that process. These choices make motif handling and the diffusion procedure work together, rather than treating chemical structure preservation as an unrelated final check.

The authors report tenfold fewer diffusion steps than existing methods and an average three percent improvement in SMILES validity over DiGress across the real-world benchmarks studied. They also report roughly four percent better motif conservation than DeFoG, supported by ChEMBL-likeness, QED, and a newly introduced shingles-distance measure. The findings concern generation efficiency, structural validity, and conservation of molecular motifs.
neurips-2025-dmol-a-highly-efficient-and.tldr: DMol combines motif compression with coordinated graph diffusion to reduce generation steps and improve reported molecular validity and motif conservation.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting represents scenes using Gaussian primitives, often requiring millions of them. Redundant primitives increase memory and rendering costs. This paper addresses compaction by treating the scene as a Gaussian mixture that should be reduced globally, rather than deciding which individual primitives to remove using heuristic importance scores.

The method uses an optimal transport perspective to compare and reduce these representations. It first minimizes a composite transport divergence over a KD-tree partition to produce compact geometry. It then separates appearance adjustment from geometry reduction, fine-tuning colors and opacity for the much smaller collection of remaining primitives.

On the evaluated benchmarks, retaining only ten percent of the Gaussians produces negligible rendering-quality loss relative to vanilla Gaussian Splatting, measured using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. The method also consistently outperforms the compared compaction techniques. Its stated applicability at any stage of vanilla or accelerated pipelines makes it a broadly compatible way to reduce representation size while preserving observed image quality.
neurips-2025-gaussian-herding-across-pen.tldr: An optimal transport approach compresses Gaussian Splatting scenes to ten percent of their primitives with negligible rendering-quality loss on tested benchmarks.

paragraphs: Graph pooling reduces the size of graphs processed by neural networks, making training faster and potentially improving generalization. However, optimizing pooling only for a prediction task can discard meaningful graph structure. This paper develops pooling layers that explicitly account for structure while repeatedly shrinking a graph through edge collapses.

The approach uses diffusion geometry to preserve the graph's metric relationships and structural diversity. A diversity measure called magnitude guides how much fidelity the pooling process retains. Because magnitude is invariant under transformations that preserve distances, it provides a geometrically grounded criterion. The authors also use spread as a faster, more stable alternative for computational efficiency.

Experiments report top performance against alternative pooling layers across diverse graph-classification tasks. The pooled graphs preserve key spectral properties, and classification accuracy remains high across different pooling ratios. These results connect predictive performance with structural preservation: the method can substantially reduce graph size while retaining properties that characterize the input's organization, rather than evaluating pooling quality through classification alone.
neurips-2025-geometry-aware-edge-pooling.tldr: Geometry-guided edge pooling shrinks graphs while preserving structural properties and maintaining strong classification performance across pooling ratios.

paragraphs: Bayesian Personalized Ranking, or BPR, is widely used as a loss function in graph self-supervised learning for recommendation. This paper examines what kinds of graph relationships that objective actually captures. Using developments in latent hyperbolic geometry, the authors connect its behavior to the paths and connectivity patterns present in a graph.

Their analysis identifies a reliance on local connectivity through two-hop paths, which leaves broader connectivity and topology insufficiently represented. They propose BPR+, a loss function that incorporates even-hop paths to capture more global relationships. The intended benefit is a more detailed assessment of how users and items relate through the surrounding graph structure.

Empirical evaluation across five real-world datasets supports BPR+ as an improvement to graph self-supervised learning frameworks. The authors also explore drug repositioning as another application, highlighting potential relevance beyond recommendation. The contribution combines an explanation of a widely used objective's limitations with a replacement designed around the structural information that the analysis finds missing.
neurips-2025-graph-theoretic-insights-in.tldr: BPR+ extends ranking objectives beyond local two-hop connectivity to capture broader graph relationships, with empirical support across five datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether large language models can provide competitive lossless image compression, where the original image must be recoverable without losing information. The authors first find that simply applying an LLM as an image compressor leaves a substantial performance gap against established codecs on common benchmarks. Strong language modeling alone does not deliver the desired image-compression results in that setup.

Their proposed model, P-LLM, focuses on predicting the next pixel in a sequence. It combines pixel-level prior information, the model's ability to use context, and a strategy intended to preserve pixel-level semantics. These components are designed to improve how the language model interprets pixel sequences and therefore improve its predictions.

Benchmark experiments show that P-LLM can outperform both classical and learned state-of-the-art codecs. The result supports adapting LLM-based prediction specifically to image structure, rather than expecting the naive application to suffice. The paper's practical contribution is the combination of image-aware methods that turns next-pixel prediction into stronger measured lossless compression.
neurips-2025-large-language-models-for-l.tldr: P-LLM adapts language-model next-pixel prediction to image structure and can outperform leading lossless codecs on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language models can be disrupted by adversarial image changes that are difficult to perceive. Improving resistance to these changes can also make it harder to preserve performance on ordinary inputs and across downstream tasks. CoAPT addresses this balance through collaborative adversarial prompt tuning that draws guidance from the original pretrained model.

The approach first uses an improved real-time total variation algorithm to suppress high-frequency image details while retaining edge structure. This step is intended to disrupt the space in which adversarial perturbations operate. It then restores natural features damaged by the processing, guided by high-level image and text representations in the pretrained model's latent space.

These two stages connect perturbation suppression with recovery of useful visual information. Experiments on four benchmarks report a strong trade-off among ordinary-input generalization, adversarial robustness, and task-specific adaptation compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using pretrained latent representations as a guide for robust learning while retaining the generalization capabilities that make those models useful.
neurips-2025-learning-robust-vision-lang.tldr: CoAPT suppresses adversarial image details and restores useful features using pretrained representations, improving the tested balance between robustness and generalization.

paragraphs: ReLoc approaches code generation as a sequence of revisions to an existing candidate program. The paper identifies efficiency and scalability problems in methods that construct programs through expanding search trees, as well as weak guidance in existing improvement-based methods. Its goal is to make revision a systematic search process with more informative candidate evaluation.

The framework has four components: drafting initial code, generating neighboring revisions, evaluating candidates, and updating the current solution. Different decision rules turn these components into search algorithms such as hill climbing or a genetic algorithm. This shared organization makes several revision strategies instances of the same framework rather than unrelated procedures.

A specialized revision reward model evaluates code quality using revision distance to produce fine-grained preferences among candidates. These preferences guide the search toward more promising changes. Across diverse code-generation tasks, experiments report superior performance over both construction-based tree search and state-of-the-art improvement-based methods. The results support combining structured local revision with feedback designed specifically to distinguish the quality of revisions.
neurips-2025-let-s-revise-step-by-step-a.tldr: ReLoc combines structured local code revision with a revision-aware reward model to outperform tested construction-based and improvement-based generation methods.

paragraphs: Lithography transfers circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers through the interaction of light, masks, and photochemical materials. Simulation connects circuit design to manufacturing, and its speed and accuracy affect downstream pattern-enhancement methods. LithoSim addresses a data problem for machine-learning simulators: insufficient coverage of process variation and mask-correction rules can leave them with inadequate understanding of lithographic behavior.

The benchmark contains more than four million high-resolution input-output pairs with physically grounded correspondence. It includes varying optical source distributions, metal and via mask patterns, optical proximity correction variants, and process windows that reflect realistic fabrication variation. This breadth makes manufacturing conditions part of the evaluation rather than treating all examples as one fixed process.

LithoSim also combines machine-learning performance measures with metrics for lithographic fidelity. The resulting framework supports comparison of data-driven and physics-informed approaches on shared criteria. The authors release data, code, and pretrained models to support further simulator development, positioning the contribution as infrastructure for evaluating both computational predictions and their manufacturing relevance.
neurips-2025-lithosim-a-large-holistic-l.tldr: LithoSim provides over four million physically grounded examples and domain-specific evaluation tools for machine-learning lithography simulation.

paragraphs: LongVPO trains vision-language models originally designed for short contexts to understand very long videos without long-video annotations. It uses two stages of Direct Preference Optimization, building synthetic examples that teach the model to prefer appropriate responses. The training progresses from locating relevant short-video evidence to reasoning across multiple video segments.

In the first stage, questions are anchored to individual clips, which are mixed with distractor clips. Visual-similarity and question-specificity filtering reduce positional bias and ambiguity. To lower computational overhead, the reference model scores only the anchor clip as an approximation to scoring the full long context.

In the second stage, recursive captioning produces scene-level metadata from long videos. A language model uses this material to generate multi-segment reasoning questions and dispreferred responses. With 16,000 synthetic examples and no costly human labels, LongVPO outperforms state-of-the-art open-source models on multiple long-video benchmarks while retaining strong short-video performance. The results support a staged synthetic-data route from local evidence selection to broader temporal reasoning.
neurips-2025-longvpo-from-anchored-cues-.tldr: LongVPO uses two stages of synthetic preference training to improve long-video understanding without long-video annotations.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis estimates the leading direction of variation as data arrives. This paper asks how accurately that direction can be learned when numerical representations have limited precision. It establishes an information-theoretic lower bound on the quantization resolution needed to achieve a chosen accuracy for the leading eigenvector.

The authors then analyze low-precision versions of Oja's algorithm using linear and nonlinear stochastic quantization. Both the weight vector and its updates are quantized using unbiased randomness. Under mild assumptions on distributional moments and the spectral gap, a batched version matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors for both quantization schemes.

For nonlinear quantization, the resulting quantization error is nearly independent of dimension. This makes the relationship between precision and accuracy especially relevant when the input has many dimensions. Experiments on synthetic data streams support the theoretical analysis and show that the low-precision methods closely follow standard Oja performance. The contribution therefore combines a fundamental precision requirement with algorithms that nearly attain it under the stated assumptions.
neurips-2025-low-precision-streaming-pca.tldr: Quantized streaming PCA nearly attains a theoretical precision lower bound under stated assumptions, with nearly dimension-free error for nonlinear quantization.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction quantifies uncertainty using prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Its efficient split variant calibrates a model using held-out data. Those guarantees depend on calibration and test observations being exchangeable, a condition that distribution shifts can violate. When this happens, the intended coverage can deteriorate.

The paper studies that deterioration through optimal transport, using unlabeled data to address the shifted setting. Existing mitigation approaches described by the authors require prior information about the kind of shift expected at test time. Their proposed perspective aims to estimate coverage loss and mitigate arbitrary distribution shifts without first restricting attention to one anticipated shift type.

The central contribution is therefore a way to reason about how distribution change affects calibrated uncertainty, together with a route to reducing its effects. The stated result concerns estimating and mitigating coverage loss; it does not turn ordinary split conformal guarantees into unconditional guarantees under every shift. This distinction matters because the original exchangeability condition remains the reason standard calibration can fail.
neurips-2025-non-exchangeable-conformal-.tldr: An optimal transport perspective enables estimation and mitigation of conformal coverage loss under distribution shift using unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper addresses two forms of language-model hallucination: failures of factual correctness and failures to remain faithful to the information being used. Methods that target these problems separately can create trade-offs, improving one while worsening the other. The authors investigate whether the model's internal representations offer a common point of intervention.

Their empirical and theoretical analysis finds overlapping activation subspaces associated with the two hallucination categories. SPACE builds on this overlap by editing shared subspaces to improve both properties together. It uses dual-task feature modeling to establish a geometric foundation for their existence, then combines spectral clustering with attention-head saliency scoring to identify and edit them.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report superior results for this unified approach. The significance is that the two problems need not always be treated as independent targets: shared internal structure can provide an opportunity for concurrent mitigation. SPACE turns that observation into a concrete intervention strategy, linking an analysis of activation geometry to changes intended to improve both factuality and faithfulness.
neurips-2025-one-space-to-rule-them-all-.tldr: SPACE edits shared activation subspaces to jointly reduce factuality and faithfulness hallucinations, addressing trade-offs from separate interventions.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning an unknown distribution over binary vectors whose coordinates are independent. Given independent samples, the learner must recover a distribution close to the original in total variation distance. Without additional advice, learning to accuracy epsilon requires at least order d divided by epsilon squared samples, where d is the number of coordinates.

The authors give the learner another product distribution as advice. Its coordinate means may be imperfect estimates of the target means. They provide an efficient algorithm whose sample complexity is approximately d to the power of one minus eta, divided by epsilon squared, with logarithmic factors suppressed, when the advice meets a specified closeness condition.

Specifically, the sum of absolute differences between the two mean vectors must be below epsilon times d raised to one-half minus an order-eta term. The algorithm does not need an advance bound on this discrepancy. The result shows that sufficiently accurate advice can reduce the dimensional dependence of sample requirements even when its accuracy is not known beforehand.
neurips-2025-product-distribution-learni.tldr: Sufficiently close product-distribution advice reduces learning sample complexity without requiring the learner to know the advice's accuracy beforehand.

paragraphs: This paper formalizes the problem of selecting the purest quantum state from several unknown candidates, motivated by identifying systems less affected by noise. The learner has K candidate states, each containing n qubits, and a total budget of N state copies. The question is how measurement choices affect the probability of selecting incorrectly.

For incoherent strategies, the authors give an adaptive algorithm with an exponentially decreasing error bound whose exponent contains a factor of two to the n in the denominator. They also construct a coherent measurement protocol whose stated exponent lacks that dimension factor. The bounds involve different quantities, H1 and H2, and establish a significant separation between the measurement settings.

A further lower bound applies specifically to strategies using fixed, two-outcome incoherent measurements, demonstrating a corresponding restriction on their achievable error. Together, these results quantify the value of coherent measurement and quantum memory for this identification problem. The contribution provides theoretical foundations and protocols aimed at improving noise-aware selection in quantum computing and communication.
neurips-2025-purest-quantum-state-identi.tldr: The paper develops purest-state identification algorithms and proves a significant advantage for coherent quantum measurements over incoherent strategies.

paragraphs: Real-DRL enables a deep reinforcement learning agent to learn during operation in safety-critical physical systems. It organizes learning around three interacting components: a student that learns action policies, a physics-based teacher responsible for safety-critical functions, and a trigger that manages their interaction. This arrangement connects ongoing policy improvement with a dedicated safety mechanism.

The teacher provides a real-time patch that both backs up plant safety and teaches the student. The student combines self-learning with learning from this intervention, while its experience sampling depends on safety status. That sampling addresses imbalances associated with corner cases, and the framework prioritizes learning safety before pursuing higher performance.

The authors present assured safety and the ability to address unexpected conditions and simulation-to-reality gaps as features of the framework. Experiments include a physical quadruped, a quadruped in Nvidia Isaac Gym, and a cart-pole system, alongside comparisons and ablations. These evaluations support the effectiveness of coordinating physics-based safety actions with a student that continues learning at runtime.
neurips-2025-real-drl-teach-and-learn-at.tldr: Real-DRL coordinates a learning agent, physics-based safety teacher, and trigger to support safety-first policy learning during operation.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic models combine neural perception with symbolic reasoning, but satisfying logical constraints does not necessarily mean they learned the intended concepts. A model can instead exploit correlations that let incorrect internal concepts produce acceptable answers. This paper addresses that failure by grounding learned concepts in a small collection of labeled examples.

The proposed architectures use prototypical learning: similarity to labeled examples helps guide which concepts the model should recognize. Training jointly accounts for this similarity and satisfaction of background knowledge. The authors demonstrate that this combination can avoid reasoning shortcuts, connecting correct symbolic outputs to learning the correct basic concepts even when supervision is extremely scarce.

Evaluation uses the rsbench suite across multiple settings, including the synthetic MNIST-EvenOdd and Kand-Logic tasks and the real-world BDD-OIA task. The authors report significant improvements in learning the intended concepts. These findings support prototype grounding as an annotation-efficient strategy for more reliable neurosymbolic learning, with concept quality itself serving as a central outcome rather than logical constraint satisfaction alone.
neurips-2025-right-for-the-right-reasons.tldr: Grounding neurosymbolic concepts in a few labeled prototypes helps models avoid reasoning shortcuts and learn intended concepts under scarce supervision.

paragraphs: SRHand reconstructs detailed hand geometry and textured images from low-resolution inputs. Hands are challenging because they deform and articulate, so methods designed for static scenes cannot simply ensure consistency across changing poses. Existing detailed reconstruction methods also rely heavily on high-resolution images from multiple viewpoints.

The method combines an implicit image representation with an explicit three-dimensional hand mesh. Its geometry-aware implicit image function learns detailed hand priors while enlarging coarse input images. Jointly optimizing that function and the hand shape connects image enhancement to geometry, helping the resulting images stay consistent across viewpoints and poses.

This coordinated optimization produces fine geometric details such as wrinkles and nails. Experiments on InterHand2.6M and Goliath report significant quantitative and qualitative improvements over state-of-the-art image-upscaling methods adapted to hands and over three-dimensional hand reconstruction methods. The findings show the value of solving image enhancement and shape recovery together when the subject is deformable, rather than treating enhanced images as independent views of an unchanged object.
neurips-2025-srhand-super-resolving-hand.tldr: SRHand jointly enhances low-resolution hand images and explicit meshes to reconstruct fine details consistently across viewpoints and poses.

paragraphs: Distributed training often combines tensor parallelism with pipeline parallelism. Tensor parallelism incurs collective communication overhead, while pipeline parallelism leaves devices waiting during synchronization gaps known as bubbles. This paper argues that treating these scheduling problems separately misses opportunities to reduce idle time across both forms of parallelism.

The proposed schedule splits pipeline forward and backward passes into fine-grained computation units. It then interleaves these units into a composite sequence designed to nearly eliminate tensor-parallelism-related bubbles. Building on that sequence, the authors further arrange the pipeline schedule to minimize its own bubbles, making the two scheduling decisions work together.

Experiments report training-throughput gains of up to twelve percent for large language models and sixteen percent for multimodal large language models relative to existing schedules. These are maximum reported improvements, rather than uniform gains for every setting. The contribution shows how reorganizing computation can improve the efficiency of combined parallel training by addressing communication-related and pipeline-related waiting within a shared schedule.
neurips-2025-synergistic-tensor-and-pipe.tldr: A coordinated tensor-and-pipeline schedule reduces both kinds of idle time, improving training throughput by up to twelve percent for LLMs and sixteen percent for multimodal LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether language-model reasoning can extend beyond the mathematics, programming, and logic tasks that have dominated prior work. It introduces ether0, a chemistry model that reasons in natural language and can answer with chemical structures. The broader question is whether scientific reasoning can be developed through post-training without additional domain pretraining.

Ether0 is a twenty-four-billion-parameter model based on Mistral-Small-24B. It is trained with reinforcement learning on 577,790 chemistry tasks grounded in experiments involving synthesized organic molecules. The approach uses extra thought tokens before answering and requires substantially less data than contemporary domain-specific models, according to the authors.

The paper reports that ether0 outperforms previous general-purpose chemistry models, frontier models, and humans in its evaluation, while also being more data-efficient than specialized models. These findings support chemistry as a domain where reasoning-focused post-training can be effective. The authors anticipate extending the method to predictive and generative tasks in other sciences; that wider applicability is a proposed direction rather than a demonstrated result here.
neurips-2025-training-a-scientific-reaso.tldr: Ether0 develops strong chemistry reasoning through reinforcement-learning post-training without additional domain pretraining and with comparatively modest data requirements.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether poisoning or backdoors in one language model can spread to another through synthetic training data. The authors first find that synthetic-data-based training strongly resists existing attacks in their evaluations. They attribute this resistance primarily to differences between the distribution of poisoned data and the clean queries used to generate synthetic examples.

They then introduce Virus Infection Attack, or VIA, to investigate whether that protection can be overcome. At a high level, VIA conceals a poisoning payload within a protective shell and searches for places in benign samples where it can influence generation. The framework is designed to propagate existing attacks even when synthetic-data queries themselves are clean.

Experiments covering both poisoning and backdoor attacks find substantially more poisoned content in generated data. Downstream models consequently reach attack success rates comparable to those of the poisoned upstream models. The findings show that resistance to conventional attacks does not establish resistance to attacks specifically adapted to synthetic-data transfer, exposing a security concern in model-to-model training pipelines.
neurips-2025-virus-infection-attack-on-l.tldr: VIA shows that poisoning and backdoors can propagate through synthetic training data even when the generation queries are clean.
